
```{r}
#| label: options
#| include: false
options(housepi.footer.warranty = TRUE)
options(housepi.footer.sample = TRUE)
```

Here we show how to check whether inference recovers the parameters used to simulate a dataset, at the same time checking how that changes with the sample size.
The simulation study of [Get started](housepi.html) does this once: a single replicate can miss the truth by chance, while many of them show whether it misses systematically.
A recovery check simulates many studys at known parameter values, fits each one back with the same model, and compares the estimates with the truth.

We use the same final-size example presented in [Get started](housepi.html):

```{r}
#| label: inference-setup
# repeat inference as in 'Get Started'
library(housepi)
set_housepi_theme()
set.seed(42)

hhmodel <- flu_1918_frederick |>
  new_housepi_model("final-size") |>
  add_parameter(import = "template")

# store posterior draws
results <- hhmodel |>
  run_inference(progress = FALSE)

results
```

The posterior above is used to estimate the model parameters.
We ask whether inference process on a target study like the considered one, generated at those very values, would let inference find them again.

# Would this study recover its own estimates?

Passing the fit as `truth` simulates at its point estimates.
Without it, the check simulates at the `value` pins of the parameter definitions, which is how to test values of your own choosing.

Each study is generated on households drawn with replacement from the attached data by `sample_house_structure()`, so it keeps the original household-size distribution, while the model draws who gets infected.
Besides the observed number of households, we ask what a quarter, half and twice as many would give:

```{r}
#| label: house-counts
# number of households in target data
n_houses <- length(unique(flu_1918_frederick$hhid))
# household sample sizes for power analysis
houses <- round(n_houses * c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2))
houses
```

# How many households?

A check costs one fit per replicate and household sample size, and larger studys take longer to fit.
We can run different replicates at each sample size using `run_parameter_recovery_check`:

```{r}
#| label: sweep
recovery <- hhmodel |>
  run_parameter_recovery_check(truth = results, nrep = 15, houses = houses,
                               progress = FALSE)
recovery

# wall-clock of the sampling loop, averaged over the replicates
recovery$overview
```

```{r}
#| label: sweep-cost
#| include: false
sweep_minutes <- with(recovery$overview, sum(nrep * mean_inference_secs)) / 60
```

Before running longer checks, it is useful to note how slower are the fits for the largest sample sizes.
Here the `r sum(recovery$overview$nrep)` fits took `r round(sweep_minutes, 1)` minutes on one thread, from `r round(min(recovery$overview$mean_inference_secs), 1)` seconds each at `r min(houses)` households to `r round(max(recovery$overview$mean_inference_secs), 1)` seconds at `r max(houses)`.

A fit whose draws do not pass the convergence diagnostics is counted as flagged: here `r sum(recovery$overview$n_flagged)` of `r sum(recovery$overview$nrep)`.
A few flags among many clean fits are expected from a finite sampler; flags concentrated at one household count call for more `steps` at that size.

## At the observed size

Each credible interval against the value that generated its study, at the `r n_houses` households of Frederick:

```{r}
#| label: recovery-plot
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Three panels, one per parameter. Each shows credible intervals,
#|  one per replicate, around a horizontal line at the true value.
#|  Intervals that miss the line are drawn in orange.
library(ggplot2)

recovery$estimates |>
  dplyr::filter(houses == n_houses) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rep, y = estimate)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = cri_lower, ymax = cri_upper, colour = covers)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = truth)) +
  # tell the intervals that miss the truth
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "black", `FALSE` = "coral"),
                      labels = c(`TRUE` = "covers truth",
                                 `FALSE` = "misses truth")) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Replicate", y = "Estimate", colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: observed-size
#| include: false
observed <- subset(recovery$summary, houses == n_houses)
rownames(observed) <- observed$variable
```

A reasonable recovery check shows intervals scattered around the target line, whereas intervals stacked on one side of it would be bias.
At this size the 95% intervals cover the truth in `r round(100 * observed["alpha", "coverage"])`% of the replicates for `alpha`, `r round(100 * observed["beta", "coverage"])`% for `beta`, and `r round(100 * observed["gamma", "coverage"])`% for `gamma`.

## Bias across sizes

The error of every estimate relative to the truth, at each household count, is distributed as follows:

```{r}
#| label: bias-plot
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Three panels, one per parameter, on a shared vertical axis. Each shows
#|  one box per household count over the relative error of the estimates, against a line at zero.
recovery$estimates |>
  dplyr::mutate(rel_error = estimate / truth - 1) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(houses), y = rel_error)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable) +
  labs(x = "Number of households", y = "Relative error")
```

Each box spans the middle half of the estimates, so it shows how far a single study of that size lands from the truth.
A box that narrows as households are added is a study buying precision, and one that stays off zero while it narrows is an estimator centered on the wrong value.

## What a larger study buys

A larger study costs more to collect, and more to fit.
We put the width of the credible interval on each parameter next to the time of one fit, and to the effective sample size (ESS) it draws per second.
A fit is only as usable as its worst-mixing parameter, so the ESS is the smallest bulk ESS over the parameters:

```{r}
#| label: design-table
vars <- names(recovery$truth)

recovery$summary |>
  dplyr::select(houses, variable, cri_width) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = cri_width) |>
  dplyr::left_join(recovery$overview[c("houses", "mean_inference_secs",
                                       "mean_min_ess_per_sec")],
                   by = "houses") |>
  dplyr::mutate(mean_min_ess_per_sec = as.integer(mean_min_ess_per_sec)) |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::colformat_double(digits = 3) |>
  flextable::colformat_double(j = "mean_inference_secs", digits = 1) |>
  flextable::add_header_row(values = c("", "CrI width", "", ""),
                            colwidths = c(1, length(vars), 1, 1)) |>
  flextable::labelizor(
    labels = c(houses = "n. households",
               mean_inference_secs = "seconds per fit",
               mean_min_ess_per_sec = "min ESS per second")
  ) |>
  flextable::align(align = "center", part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit()
```

```{r}
#| label: doubling
#| include: false
width <- tidyr::pivot_wider(recovery$summary[c("houses", "variable", "cri_width")],
                            names_from = houses, values_from = cri_width)
narrower <- 1 - width[[as.character(2 * n_houses)]] / width[[as.character(n_houses)]]
secs <- setNames(recovery$overview$mean_inference_secs,
                 recovery$overview$houses)
slower <- secs[[as.character(2 * n_houses)]] / secs[[as.character(n_houses)]] - 1
```

Doubling Frederick to `r 2 * n_houses` households narrows the intervals by `r round(100 * min(narrower))`% - `r round(100 * max(narrower))`%, but makes a fit `r round(100 * slower)`% slower.
